paragraphs: This paper gives a shared mathematical interpretation of three methods for reducing the dimensionality of manifold data: Isomap, graph Laplacian eigenmaps, and locally linear embedding. Each method starts from relationships within local neighborhoods and uses them to construct a global embedding. The paper asks how these apparently different procedures fit into the same framework.

The central result is that all three can be described as kernel principal component analysis applied to specially constructed Gram matrices. These matrices encode the relationships used by the embedding procedure. Under this interpretation, the choice of matrix becomes the place where the distinctive behavior of each algorithm enters the common kernel framework.

Representative examples illustrate both similarities and differences among the algorithms. The contribution is a way to understand existing methods together: their common kernel formulation clarifies what they share, while their different matrix constructions retain their individual approaches to turning local information into global geometry.
icml-2004-a-kernel-view-of-the-dimension.tldr: Isomap, Laplacian eigenmaps, and LLE can all be understood as kernel PCA with specially constructed Gram matrices.

paragraphs: This paper extends Isomap to data whose observations have both spatial and temporal relationships. Its method, ST-Isomap, brings those two kinds of information into the dimensionality reduction process. This is relevant when observations belong to an unfolding sequence, so their relationships include how they follow one another as well as how they are arranged in the input space.

ST-Isomap incorporates temporal relationships into local neighborhoods within the existing Isomap framework. A shortest-path mechanism then propagates this local information globally. The resulting construction allows temporal relationships to contribute to the overall embedding through the same neighborhood-to-global pathway used to organize the data.

The paper presents two versions, addressing sequentially continuous data and segmented data. It also reports applications to real-world observations from human motion performance and humanoid robot teleoperation. These applications demonstrate the proposed extension in settings involving movement over time, while the two versions accommodate different forms of temporal organization.
icml-2004-a-spatio-temporal-extension-to.tldr: ST-Isomap incorporates temporal relationships into local neighborhoods and propagates them globally to embed spatial and temporal data.

paragraphs: Feature selection with a linear support vector machine often treats small feature weights as evidence that the corresponding variables can be removed. This paper examines the theoretical basis of that practice. It establishes that, in the sample limit, theoretically irrelevant variables receive zero weight in both soft-margin and hard-margin linear SVMs.

That result does not make SVM weights a complete description of feature relevance. The authors construct examples in which strongly relevant variables receive zero weight, even though they are needed for optimal estimation of the target distribution. They also show that weakly relevant variables can receive nonzero weights despite being unnecessary for optimal feature selection when other features are available.

The paper compares these properties with Markov-blanket approaches to feature selection. For a broad class of distributions, those approaches avoid the identified disadvantages and may also support causal discovery. The findings distinguish a useful guarantee about irrelevant variables from stronger interpretations of SVM weights that the counterexamples undermine.
icml-2004-a-theoretical-characterization.tldr: Linear SVMs give irrelevant variables zero weight in the sample limit, but their weights can still misrepresent other forms of feature relevance.

paragraphs: The paper studies authorship verification: given writing from one known author, determine whether a long text was written by that person. This framing makes the available examples of a single author's writing central to the task. The proposed learning method measures how deeply two sets of examples differ.

Its key procedure repeatedly removes the strongest features from the learning process and tracks how quickly the accuracy of learned models declines. The rate of degradation provides information beyond the accuracy obtained with all features present. It makes the persistence of a learned distinction under feature removal part of the evidence used to assess the two example sets.

The authors present evidence that this approach achieves very high accuracy on the authorship verification problem. The stated finding supports examining the behavior of learned models as their best features disappear. The contribution is therefore both an authorship verification method and a particular way of probing the depth of differences between example collections.
icml-2004-authorship-verification-as-a-o.tldr: The method verifies authorship by measuring how model accuracy deteriorates as the strongest distinguishing features are repeatedly removed.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bellman update for reinforcement learning in relational domains. The proposed operator, ReBel, is designed to work with a compact description of a Markov decision process expressed in a constraint logic programming language. The representation makes relational structure part of the machinery used to describe the decision problem.

Using ReBel, the authors construct a value iteration algorithm in which abstraction over both states and actions has a central role. The contribution connects the representation of the problem with the operation used to update values. State and action abstraction are therefore part of how the algorithm performs its reasoning about the relational decision process.

The paper presents convergence results and experiments, alongside the new operator and algorithm. Its significance is a concrete framework for bringing relational representations into Bellman-style computation. The theoretical results address convergence within that framework, while the experiments provide an additional examination of the proposed approach to relational reinforcement learning.
icml-2004-bellman-goes-relational-b01150.tldr: ReBel combines a relational Bellman update with state and action abstraction to support value iteration on compactly represented decision processes.

paragraphs: This paper adapts boosting to grammatical inference, with the aim of improving state merging algorithms when training data contain noise. The central concern is how boosting should use examples whose labels have different levels of reliability. The proposed approach introduces additional information from an oracle into the update rule.

To use that information, the authors construct a weighting scheme that accounts for confidence in each example's label. Confidence thus influences the weights used during learning and becomes part of the boosting process itself. This directly connects the treatment of noisy labels with the mechanism used to update the importance of training examples.

The authors prove that the resulting framework preserves the theoretical properties of boosting. They also evaluate it with the state merging algorithm RPNI* on several datasets and report dramatic performance improvements. Together, these contributions provide theoretical support for the modified framework and empirical evidence that label-confidence information can improve grammatical inference in the studied noisy-data setting.
icml-2004-boosting-grammatical-inference.tldr: A confidence-aware boosting scheme improves grammatical inference with noisy labels while preserving boosting's theoretical properties.

paragraphs: Graph-based clustering depends heavily on the distance function used to compare neighboring points. This paper learns that function through binary classification of point pairs. A classifier predicts whether two points belong to the same class, and its signed margin supplies the distance value used in clustering.

The main method, DistBoost, combines boosted hypotheses over pairs of points with a weak learner that partitions the original feature space. Each weak hypothesis is a Gaussian mixture model fitted through a semi-supervised constrained expectation-maximization procedure. This allows both labeled and unlabeled data to contribute. The paper also considers SVMs and boosted decision trees as margin-based classifiers of pairs.

Experiments compare the learned distances with other metric learning methods and approaches that insert constraints directly into clustering algorithms. Evaluations include UCI datasets, a sample of MNIST, and animal color images. DistBoost significantly and robustly outperforms its competitors in most reported cases, supporting the usefulness of learning pairwise relationships for these clustering tasks.
icml-2004-boosting-margin-based-distance.tldr: DistBoost learns clustering distances from boosted pairwise classifiers and significantly outperforms competitors in most reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper builds decision trees around the combined cost of classification mistakes and obtaining information. The objective reflects diagnostic tasks in which making an incorrect decision has a cost, but measuring an attribute can also require payment or effort. The authors introduce a splitting criterion that accounts for both costs when selecting attributes during tree construction.

They also address prediction when test cases have many missing values. Several proposed strategies suggest which missing values to obtain, taking acquisition costs into account. This extends cost-sensitive reasoning beyond tree construction to the decisions made while using the tree on an incomplete case.

Experiments compare the proposed strategies with C4.5 and its variations, reporting significant improvements. The authors also state that their algorithm has complexity similar to C4.5 and substantially below previous work. The practical contribution is an approach that considers the expense of acquiring information together with the expense of mistakes, both when building a tree and when applying it.
icml-2004-decision-trees-with-minimal-co.tldr: The proposed decision-tree methods account for both misclassification and information-acquisition costs during training and prediction.

paragraphs: This paper examines an entropy-based objective for clustering categorical data. Entropy-type measures have long been used to describe how heterogeneous a cluster is. The authors investigate the mathematical basis of such a criterion and how it can guide the search for a partition of the data into clusters.

They show that the criterion can be derived within a formal probabilistic clustering framework. They also establish a connection with clustering approaches based on dissimilarity coefficients. These results relate the entropy objective to two ways of describing clustering: through a probability model and through measures of differences between observations.

The paper then presents an iterative Monte Carlo procedure for searching for partitions that minimize the criterion. Experiments show the effectiveness of the proposed procedure. The contribution combines an explanation of why the objective arises with a method for pursuing it computationally, linking the interpretation of cluster heterogeneity to an operational search over possible groupings.
icml-2004-entropy-based-criterion-in-cat.tldr: The paper grounds entropy-based categorical clustering in probabilistic models and proposes a Monte Carlo procedure to optimize the criterion.

paragraphs: The paper extends graph kernels that make kernel methods applicable to labeled graphs, including graphs representing chemical compounds. These kernels compare paths and combine those comparisons according to random walks along graph edges. The authors seek changes that both reduce computation time and make the resulting graph similarities more relevant.

The first extension enriches each vertex label with information about its surrounding environment using the Morgan algorithm. This adds local context to the information available for comparison. The second changes the random walk model so that a walk cannot immediately return to the vertex it just visited, modifying which paths contribute to the graph comparison.

Both extensions are tested in benchmark experiments on chemical compound classification, with promising results. The contribution operates at two different levels of the same kernel construction: the information attached to individual vertices and the behavior of the walks connecting them. These changes offer ways to refine the representation and path sampling underlying graph similarity.
icml-2004-extensions-of-marginalized-gra.tldr: Two graph-kernel extensions enrich vertex labels and prevent immediate random-walk backtracking, with promising chemical classification results.

paragraphs: LASSO combines coefficient shrinkage with variable selection, making it useful when a model should reduce the influence of some inputs and exclude others. This paper addresses the computational burden of fitting such a model. The authors identify quadratic programming and general nonlinear programming approaches to the L1-penalized problem as computationally intensive.

They propose a gradient descent algorithm for LASSO that is computationally simpler than those optimization approaches. The intended benefit is applicability to large problems. This comes with an explicit tradeoff: the authors describe the final result as slightly less accurate, so the computational simplification is accompanied by a modest loss in accuracy.

The paper provides a convergence rate for the algorithm and illustrates its behavior using simulated models and real datasets. Its contribution is a simpler optimization route to LASSO's combined shrinkage and selection objective. The convergence analysis and examples support examining that route when the computational demands of the alternative formulations become a central concern.
icml-2004-gradient-lasso-for-feature-sel.tldr: Gradient LASSO trades slightly lower accuracy for a computationally simpler optimization method suited to large problems.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the assumptions behind linear classification of categorical data. It places the problem on the multinomial manifold: the simplex of multinomial probability models equipped with a geometry derived from Fisher information. This gives the classification problem a mathematical setting tied to the probability models used to describe categorical observations.

Within that setting, the authors develop a new interpretation of hyperplane classifiers and a generalized notion of margin. Together, these ideas show how existing margin-based hyperplane models can be adapted to multinomial geometry. The change concerns both the interpretation of the separating classifier and the margin used to describe its separation of classes.

Experiments show that the resulting classification framework is effective for text classification, where multinomial models naturally represent the categorical structure of the data. The contribution connects the choice of probability model with classifier geometry, showing how a familiar margin-based approach can be reformulated to match that structure.
icml-2004-hyperplane-margin-classifiers-.tldr: The paper adapts hyperplane classifiers and their margins to multinomial geometry, with effective text-classification results.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a perceptron-based discriminative algorithm for labeling structured inputs such as sequences, trees, and graphs. The central challenge it addresses is incorporating features that involve many hidden variables. The authors contrast this goal with existing labelers, including maximum entropy Markov models and conditional random fields, that handle features involving only a small number of hidden variables.

The proposed algorithm combines a fully kernelized formulation with pointwise label prediction. According to the paper, this combination permits large features involving arbitrarily many hidden variables while retaining polynomial time complexity. These two design choices are therefore central to the stated ability to use richer features in structured labeling.

The authors also introduce kernel functions for sequences, trees, and graphs, together with efficient algorithms for computing them. The contribution includes both a learning procedure and kernels suited to its structured inputs. Its stated computational result explains why incorporating the described feature scope can remain tractable within this particular labeling framework.
icml-2004-kernel-based-discriminative-le.tldr: A kernelized perceptron labeler uses pointwise prediction to incorporate features involving arbitrarily many hidden variables in polynomial time.

paragraphs: This paper introduces kernel conditional random fields as a framework for discriminative modeling of graph-structured data. The framework brings kernels and their implicit feature spaces into conditional graphical models. It connects the representation of structured relationships with the feature representations made available by kernel methods.

A representer theorem establishes how these models arise from risk minimization using Mercer kernels on labeled graphs. The authors then propose a greedy procedure for selecting cliques in the dual representation. This selection procedure allows sparse representations, giving the framework a way to retain selected components of the model rather than requiring a dense representation.

The use of graph kernels also enables semi-supervised learning algorithms for structured data within the framework. The authors demonstrate the models and clique selection procedures on synthetic data and apply them to protein secondary structure prediction. The contribution combines a theoretical representation result, a sparsity mechanism, and demonstrations of their use in structured prediction.
icml-2004-kernel-conditional-random-fiel.tldr: Kernel conditional random fields combine implicit kernel features with graphical models and use greedy clique selection to obtain sparse representations.

paragraphs: Predictive state representations describe a controlled dynamical system using predictions about observable outcomes of tests that could be performed on it. Their parameters specify how those predictions change as actions are taken and observations arrive. Learning such a model involves choosing the tests that define state as well as estimating the dynamics.

This paper addresses both problems for linear predictive state representations in systems with a reset operation. The authors present the first discovery algorithm for selecting the tests and a new algorithm for learning model parameters. The reset requirement is part of the stated scope of these methods.

The paper reports experimental verification of the algorithms. It also distinguishes the approach from prior work on observable operator models. Against earlier parameter-learning work with mixed results and the absence of discovery results, the contribution supplies methods for both defining the predictive state and learning its evolution within the specified class of resettable systems.
icml-2004-learning-and-discovery-of-pred.tldr: The paper provides discovery and learning algorithms for linear predictive state representations in controlled systems that support resetting.

paragraphs: This paper examines why Bayesian networks trained in the standard way can perform poorly as classifiers. The authors attribute the problem to a mismatch between the training objective and the classification goal. Modeling the likelihood of the data does not directly target classification accuracy or the conditional likelihood of the class.

Optimizing both network structure and parameters for conditional likelihood is described as prohibitively expensive. The proposed approximation separates those choices: select structures by maximizing conditional likelihood, but estimate their parameters by maximum likelihood. This keeps a classification-oriented objective in the structural search while using the simpler parameter estimation approach.

On a large collection of benchmark datasets, the method produces better class probability estimates than naive Bayes, tree-augmented naive Bayes, and generatively trained Bayesian networks. These findings support the particular division of training objectives proposed by the authors. They show that a practical approximation can improve probability estimation without carrying out the prohibitively costly joint conditional optimization.
icml-2004-learning-bayesian-network-clas.tldr: Selecting Bayesian network structures by conditional likelihood while fitting parameters by maximum likelihood improves class probability estimates on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the Maxi-Min Margin Machine, called M4, as a classifier that combines local and global views of data. The authors position it alongside support vector machines and minimax probability machines, which they describe as using one or the other view. M4 brings both perspectives into a single large-margin model.

A central theoretical result is that SVMs and minimax probability machines can each be treated as special cases of M4. The authors provide a geometric interpretation and theoretical justifications for the broader formulation. They also show that optimizing M4 can be expressed as a sequential conic programming problem and propose efficient methods for solving it.

Evaluations use both synthetic datasets and real-world benchmarks. Comparisons with SVMs and minimax probability machines demonstrate advantages of the new model in those evaluations. The contribution therefore combines a unifying mathematical formulation with a practical optimization approach and empirical evidence supporting the combined local and global perspective.
icml-2004-learning-large-margin-classifi.tldr: M4 combines local and global data views in a large-margin classifier that includes SVMs and minimax probability machines as special cases.

paragraphs: This paper learns Gaussian process parameters from multiple tasks. Its key modeling assumption is that the tasks were drawn independently from the same Gaussian process prior. Under that assumption, information from separate tasks can contribute to learning the parameters of the shared prior, making the relationship among tasks part of the learning problem.

The proposed algorithm extends the informative vector machine to this multitask setting. Called MT-IVM, it saves computation by greedily choosing the most informative examples from the separate tasks. Selecting examples is therefore the mechanism used to make parameter learning across tasks computationally efficient.

The authors report two distinct comparisons. On an artificial dataset, MT-IVM is more efficient than random subsampling. On a speaker-dependent phoneme recognition task, it is more effective than the traditional informative vector machine. These findings support the proposed selection strategy and multitask extension in the evaluated settings, with the shared-prior assumption providing the basis for learning across tasks.
icml-2004-learning-to-learn-with-the-inf.tldr: MT-IVM efficiently learns shared Gaussian process parameters across tasks by greedily selecting informative examples.

paragraphs: This paper addresses boosting's sensitivity to noisy labels and outliers. The authors attribute part of that sensitivity to margin-based loss functions that are unbounded. They develop two algorithms that build on boosting while using a bounded loss of the margin, changing how the learning objective treats difficult observations.

The first algorithm alternates expectation-maximization with boosting steps. The second expresses a nonconvex loss as the difference of two convex losses. The authors prove that both algorithms converge to a stationary point. That is the stated convergence result; it does not establish that either procedure necessarily reaches a global optimum.

The paper also studies generalization through Rademacher complexity and evaluates the methods on synthetic data, optical character recognition, and text. The experiments demonstrate benefits of the framework, particularly robustness to outliers. Together, the optimization results, generalization analysis, and experiments support bounded margin losses as a way to address part of boosting's observed sensitivity to noise.
icml-2004-leveraging-the-margin-more-car.tldr: Two boosting-based algorithms use bounded margin losses, converge to stationary points, and demonstrate robustness to outliers.

paragraphs: This paper learns a common feature selection or kernel selection configuration for several support vector machines. The setting involves related tasks with differently labeled datasets over the same input space. By learning the representation jointly, the datasets can reinforce a shared choice of useful features or kernels for their respective classifiers.

The authors derive the approach using maximum entropy discrimination. The resulting algorithms jointly estimate the parameters of multiple SVM classification or regression models and an optimal feature subset or kernel combination. Individual task models therefore have their own parameters while participating in the shared representation choice.

The algorithms are convex and retain the global solution properties associated with SVMs. This is a central computational feature of the formulation because representation selection and task learning are optimized together. Experiments on standardized datasets illustrate the approach. The contribution is a framework in which related tasks can inform a common representation while preserving the stated optimization properties.
icml-2004-multi-task-feature-and-kernel-.tldr: A convex multitask method jointly learns SVM parameters and a shared feature subset or kernel combination across related datasets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces RankOpt, a linear binary classifier whose training objective targets area under the ROC curve, or AUC. The central idea is to align optimization with that statistic. Doing so creates two obstacles: AUC is nondifferentiable, and its computation has quadratic complexity in the number of observations.

RankOpt addresses both obstacles through a differentiable approximation to AUC. The authors describe this approximation as accurate and computationally efficient, with linear complexity in the number of observations. Its differentiability makes gradient descent possible, and its computational cost allows the optimization to run in reasonable time.

The paper compares RankOpt with several other linear binary classifiers across multiple classification problems. RankOpt performs significantly better in almost all of the reported cases. This empirical result supports training around the AUC objective in the tested settings. The methodological contribution is the approximation that turns a difficult statistic into a practical target for gradient-based learning.
icml-2004-optimising-area-under-the-roc-.tldr: RankOpt trains a linear classifier using an efficient differentiable AUC approximation and significantly outperforms tested alternatives in almost all cases.

paragraphs: Tangent Distance is a method for invariant pattern classification, but conventional use requires tangent vectors to be available beforehand. The paper identifies obtaining those vectors as difficult for objects beyond images. It aims to extend the approach to more general classification tasks by changing how the required variation information is represented.

The basic assumption is that pattern variations can approximately represent tangent vectors. The authors introduce three probabilistic models for encoding those variations: a linear subspace model, a nonlinear subspace model, and a manifold subspace model. They bring these alternatives together in a common framework called Probabilistic Tangent Subspace.

Experiments on non-image datasets show promising classification performance. These results support the proposed extension in settings where conventional tangent vectors are difficult to obtain. The framework's significance lies in connecting the needed tangent information to modeled pattern variations, with three related modeling choices organized under one view and the approximation assumption remaining central to the approach.
icml-2004-probabilistic-tangent-subspace.tldr: Probabilistic Tangent Subspace extends tangent-based classification by assuming pattern variations can approximate tangent vectors.

paragraphs: Feature induction creates nonlinear combinations of existing inputs and adds them as features for classification. This paper examines how to do that explicitly for support vector machines. The authors identify two concerns with nonlinear kernels: their induced feature spaces are usually high-dimensional, increasing the chance of overfitting, and their implicit features make important combinations difficult to understand.

The proposed boosting-style algorithm explicitly induces important nonlinear features for an SVM. This makes the created combinations part of the model's input representation. The approach addresses the authors' concern about identifying which induced features matter while pursuing the original goal of improving classification accuracy.

Empirical studies show that the method improves SVM classification accuracy. Comparisons with SVMs using nonlinear kernels also indicate effectiveness and robustness, particularly when training data are scarce. These findings support explicit feature induction as a useful approach in the evaluated settings, with the reported small-sample behavior especially relevant to the paper's concern about overfitting.
icml-2004-robust-feature-induction-for-s.tldr: A boosting-style algorithm explicitly creates nonlinear SVM features and shows effective, robust performance, especially with small training sets.

paragraphs: Cooperative multiagent learning becomes difficult because joint state and action spaces grow exponentially with the number of agents. This paper studies how Q-learning can learn coordinated behavior using a sparse representation of that joint space. The goal is to represent the coordination dependencies needed for a group of agents to act together.

The authors first examine a compact representation in which explicit coordination is required only in a predefined set of states. They then introduce a coordination-graph approach that represents Q-values through value rules. These rules specify which agents need to coordinate in particular states, making the dependencies depend on the situation.

The paper shows how Q-learning can efficiently learn a coordinated policy within this framework. It demonstrates the method in a predator-prey domain and compares it with related multiagent Q-learning approaches. The contribution connects sparse, state-dependent descriptions of coordination with a learning procedure, addressing the representational burden that motivates the work.
icml-2004-sparse-cooperative-q-learning-.tldr: Sparse cooperative Q-learning uses state-dependent coordination rules to learn joint behavior without a full joint-space representation.

paragraphs: This paper defines attribute interactions through dependencies that cannot be reduced to relationships among smaller parts. It extends the discussion beyond pairwise interactions to general groups of attributes. The operational question is whether a model reconstructed from the parts differs significantly from a model fitted directly to the whole group.

The authors use the Kirkwood superposition approximation to build the part-to-whole model. Comparing it with the direct model supplies a test for interaction. They then construct a model by testing which interactions are present, producing a graphical map of significant relationships learned from the data rather than assuming an interaction structure in advance.

The paper also compares significance calculations based on an asymptotic chi-squared distribution with those obtained by bootstrap. The resulting P-values closely match. This finding supports the reported significance calculations, while the broader contribution is a test-based route from an operational definition of higher-order interaction to the structure of a graphical model.
icml-2004-testing-the-significance-of-at.tldr: The paper tests higher-order attribute interactions by comparing whole-group models with reconstructions from their parts, then builds graphical models from significant interactions.
